newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche denies helping Krupp, Thyssen at same time.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche denies helping Krupp, Thyssen at same time.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG on Thursday dismissed as nonsense a magazine report that it had been advising Thyssen AG while at the same time helping Krupp AG to prepare a hostile takeover bid for the German steelmaker.
"The whole story is complete nonsense," a spokesman for the bank said in response to a Reuter enquiry.

Der Spiegel magazine reported that Deutsche's investment banking unit Deutsche Morgan Grenfell helped Thyssen to organise presentations to investors in the U.S. and Britain in February at which internal figures about Thyssen, for example its hidden reserves, were revealed.
At the same time, the magazine said, Morgan Grenfell was working out a plan for Krupp to launch a hostile takeover bid for Thyssen which was to be partly financed from Thyssen's reserves.
Der Spiegel released a summary of the article ahead of publication in its next edition.
The Deutsche Bank spokesman said Morgan Grenfell had merely given Thyssen organisational and technical help with the presentations and that the information provided there had not been confidential.
"Morgan Grenfell did not receive the consultancy contract from Krupp until after the presentations," the spokesman said.
Krupp, whose full name is Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, launched the bid last week but withdrew it on Monday after a storm of protest at what unions and politicians called "Wild West" tactics.
The two companies have since signed a basic agreement of understanding on founding a joint steel-producing company in a move that will cost 8,000 jobs.

The bank also denied a claim by Spiegel that Deutsche management board member Ulrich Cartellieri, who resigned as member of Thyssen's supervisory board on Thursday, had warned the bank against arranging a hostile takeover between two firms in which trade unions had such a dominant influence.

Deutsche incurred a barrage of criticism for its role in the aborted takeover as unions accused it of jeopardising livelihoods for financial gain and politicians called for curbs on the power of German banks.

Some 30,000 steelworkers demonstrated outside Deutsche's doors in Frankfurt on Tuesday but chief executive Hilmar Kopper remained defiant, saying he saw no basis for the attacks and that Deutsche had only been doing its job in advising Krupp.

Kopper also accused unions of hypocrisy for accusing banks of endangering jobs and then arranging a steel merger which led to the similar number of job cuts that a straight takeover would have caused.
Deutsche, Dresdner Bank AG and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs advised Krupp and agreed to finance the takeover.
Deutsche came under particular attack because Cartellieri was on Thyssen's supervisory board but never told Thyssen it was supporting a takeover by a rival.
Cartellieri this week acknowledged it was getting harder for bankers to grapple with the conflicts of interest resulting from their many supervisory board mandates.
